title: Equal Sum Arrays With Minimum Number of Operations
statement:
Two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2` are given; their lengths may differ, and every value in them lies between 1 and 6 inclusive. An operation picks any single element of either array and replaces it with any value from 1 to 6.

Return the smallest number of operations after which the elements of `nums1` add up to the same total as the elements of `nums2`. If no sequence of operations can make the two totals equal, return `-1`.
notes:
## Intuition

Only the difference between the two totals matters. Call the array with the bigger total `larger` and the other `smaller`. One operation can shrink the `gap` by at most 5: lowering a value `v` of `larger` to 1 saves `v - 1`, and raising a value `v` of `smaller` to 6 adds `6 - v`. Each element offers one such gain, and partial changes are always possible, so the greedy choice is to spend the biggest gains first. Values only range over 1 to 6, so counting gains in six buckets replaces sorting.

## Approach

1. Compute `sum1` and `sum2`, pick `larger` and `smaller`, and set `gap` to the absolute difference.
2. Fill `gains[g]`: each value `v` of `larger` adds one to bucket `v - 1`, each value `v` of `smaller` adds one to bucket `6 - v`.
3. Walk `gain` from 5 down to 1 while `gap > 0`. Take `used = min(gains[gain], ceil(gap / gain))` operations from that bucket, add them to `operations` and subtract `used * gain` from `gap`.
4. If `gap` is still positive, every gain was spent and the totals cannot meet: return `-1`. Otherwise return `operations`.

## Example 1, step by step

`sum1 = 21`, `sum2 = 10`, so `larger = nums1` and `gap = 11`. `nums1` contributes one gain each of 0 to 5; `nums2 = [1,1,2,2,2,2]` contributes 5, 5, 4, 4, 4, 4. So `gains[5] = 3`. At `gain = 5`, `used = min(3, ceil(11 / 5)) = 3`, `operations = 3`, `gap = -4`. The gap is closed (overshooting is fine, since any change can be made smaller), so the answer is 3.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m): one pass over each array, then at most five buckets.
- Space: O(1): six counters.

## Pitfalls

- Overshooting is allowed: a change can always be chosen to close exactly the remaining amount, so `ceil(gap / gain)` is right.
- A value of 1 in `larger` or 6 in `smaller` offers gain 0; never count it as an operation.
- Return `-1` only when the gains run out; a quick check is that the longer array has more than six times as many elements.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sum1`, `sum2` | totals of `nums1` and `nums2` |
| `larger`, `smaller` | the arrays with the bigger and the smaller total |
| `gap` | how much difference is still left to close |
| `gains` | `gains[g]` counts elements whose single change closes `g` |
| `gain` | the bucket currently being spent |
| `used` | operations taken from that bucket |
| `operations` | operations spent so far |

narration.6: This is the difference the operations must close.
narration.8: Six buckets, one for each possible gain from 0 to 5.
narration.10: Lowering value v to 1 closes v - 1 of the gap.
narration.13: Raising value v to 6 closes 6 - v of the gap.
narration.17: Spend the biggest gains first, stopping once the gap is closed.
narration.18: Use only as many of this bucket as the remaining gap needs.
narration.19: Each one is a single operation.
narration.20: Shrink the gap by what those operations closed.
narration.22: A leftover gap means the totals can never meet.
